🪙 A PENNY FROM HIS LUNCH CHANGE SOLD FOR $204,000

In 1947, 16-year-old Don Lutes Jr. of Pittsfield, Massachusetts, noticed something odd in the change from his high school cafeteria: a 1943 Lincoln cent that was copper-colored instead of silvery.

In 1943 the U.S. Mint made pennies from zinc-coated steel to save copper for World War II. A few leftover bronze blanks were caught in the bins that fed the presses and were struck by mistake. Lutes wrote to the Treasury, which told him copper pennies were not struck in 1943. He kept the coin anyway.

Only 10 to 15 examples of the 1943 bronze cent are known, according to Heritage Auctions. On January 10, 2019, Lutes’ coin sold at Heritage in Orlando for $204,000 after more than 30 bids. Lutes had died the previous September, and the proceeds went to Pittsfield’s public library, the Berkshire Athenaeum.

➡️From Vintage to MNTGE: Digital Fashion Brand to Release NFT Patches Linked to IRL Rewards

Digital fashion brand MNTGE is gearing up to release its Patchwork collection, comprised of a series of non-fungible token (NFT) patches paired with a physical counterpart.

MNTGE Patchwork features 13 unique digital patches designed by 11 artists including Jen Stark, Bored Ape Yacht Club artist Seneca and Nyan Cat meme creator Christopher Torres. The entire 7,500-unit collection will open for sale on July 27 on NFT marketplace OpenSea. Each NFT will be priced at 0.07 ETH, or $130, and the artwork will be revealed upon mint.

Each NFT is linked to an identical physical patch. Embedded with a near-field communication (NFC) chip, owners can scan the real-world patch to claim the digital token in their crypto wallet. By holding the patch on the blockchain and IRL, users can trace ownership as well as attend token-gated events and exclusive MNTGE experiences.

Additionally, the patches aren’t just one-off collectibles. In the physical world, they can be sewn onto MNTGE’s “base garments,” including t-shirts, jackets and denim. In the digital realm, the patches can be “owned” by the base garment itself. By implementing an ERC-6551 token standard, the digital wearable becomes a token-bound account that can custody the patches – creating an added layer of digital ownership.

Nick Adler, co-founder of MNTGE, told CoinDesk that the company was rooted in the goal of selling vintage fashion and utilizing the blockchain to revitalize its origins.

“People are out there wearing [vintage] and collecting it…young kids want to be authentic,” said Adler. “They don't want a Hot Topic shirt, they want the original shirt, right? So we just saw this natural, really honest use case for the blockchain, and we just felt like the two could really go hand in hand.”

Lately, I've been interviewing AI Engineer candidates with 1–2 years of experience.

One thing surprised me.
Almost everyone can talk about RAG.
Almost everyone has built AI agents.

Most have used LangChain, LangGraph, OpenAI, Claude, or Gemini.
But when the conversation moves beyond frameworks...
...that's where many interviews start to slow down.

I ask simple questions like:
"Why do embeddings work?"
"Why does chunk size affect retrieval?"
"Why does an attention mechanism matter?"
"What actually happens before an LLM generates the first token?"

The room usually goes quiet.
It made me realize something.
We're getting really good at building AI applications.

But we're slowly skipping the fundamentals that make those applications reliable.
AI tools can write code.
They can generate APIs.
They can even scaffold an entire project.

But they can't replace your understanding.
If retrieval quality drops...
If latency suddenly doubles...
If hallucinations increase...
If your AI agent gets stuck in a loop...

The solution isn't another framework.
It's understanding what's happening underneath.
Frameworks will change.
Models will change.
The fundamentals won't.

That's why, before every interview, I'd rather revise concepts like:
→ Transformers
→ Attention Mechanism
→ Embeddings
→ Tokenization
→ Vector Search
→ HTTP & APIs
→ System Design
→ Memory
→ Databases
→ Evaluation
→ Python fundamentals
These are the concepts that help you explain why something works, not just how to build it.

If you're preparing for AI Engineer interviews, don't spend all your time learning the next framework.
Spend some time strengthening the foundation that every framework is built on.

It looks like AI has become such a major economic force that people are now voting against its infrastructure.

In the recent U.S. elections, candidates who pledged to restrict the construction of new data centers secured key positions in several states. Texas is particularly interesting, as it accounts for roughly a quarter of all planned new data center capacity in the United States. The state's incoming governor has already promised to pause permits for new projects until additional industry regulations are put in place.

The reason is fairly straightforward. AI requires enormous amounts of electricity, water, and infrastructure. People are starting to feel the impact not in Nvidia's earnings reports, but in their own electricity bills, the strain on power grids, and massive construction projects taking place right next to their homes. Goldman Sachs estimates that new political restrictions could potentially affect around 45% of planned data center capacity growth in the United States.

And today, this story has already hit the markets. At one point, the S&P 500 was down more than 3%, while the Nasdaq fell around 5%. Companies tied to AI infrastructure have been hit particularly hard. Nvidia was down more than 8%, AMD around 16%, and CoreWeave around 15%. The Nasdaq has now pulled back more than 10% from its October peak.

Of course, elections aren't the only factor. Investors are increasingly questioning when the hundreds of billions of dollars currently being poured into data centers, chips, and electricity will start generating comparable returns. And now, alongside the economic question, there's a political one.

For the past few years, chips were considered the main bottleneck for AI development. Then electricity, memory, and equipment became increasingly scarce. Now there's another constraint: political approval to build all this infrastructure in the first place.

And it's entirely possible that the next phase of the AI race will be determined not by who has the best model or the most GPUs, but by who actually gets permission to connect another massive data center to the power grid.

What if your body could act as an authentication key? In May 2013, Regina E. Dugan, a former director of the Defence Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), discussed a tiny ingestible vitamin microchip designed for authentication.

The pill contains a small chip and a switch. Once swallowed, stomach acids act as an electrolyte, powering the device much like an inside-out potato battery. The switch turns on and off, generating an 18-bit, ECG-like signal in the body. In effect, the body becomes the authentication token.
